claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was about ten feet of stone sold as a petrified man
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man", uncovered on October 16, 1869

claims.claim: A printed sheet listed the figure's whole length as 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: The printed sheet gave the length of the nose as 6 inches
claims.quote: length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: The printed sheet gave the width of palm as 7 inches
claims.quote: width of palm, 7 inches

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and is credited to Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT. / Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: A tent was put up and visitors were charged fifty cents to look
claims.quote: The next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant.

claims.claim: Well-diggers found the giant on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: Within days, three to five hundred visitors came each day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day as the demand for wagons and carriages dramatically increased.

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is a Bain News Service image dated 1910
claims.quote: Date: 1910 / Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: The gypsum block was cut in an Iowa quarry
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: In 1868 Hull had a roughly ten-foot gypsum block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The workmen were told the block was intended for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The stereocard view of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa dates from 1873 and is held by NYPL
claims.quote: View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa. Date: 1873 Author: Scan by NYPL

claims.claim: Both giants were fakes and both are still displayed
claims.quote: Both it and an unauthorized copy made by P. T. Barnum are still being displayed.

claims.claim: Hull confessed in December 1869, specifically on 10 December 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was carving
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: Two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York uncovered the figure
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over the giant
claims.quote: He covered the giant with a tent and it soon became an attraction site.

claims.claim: The viewing session was fifteen minutes long
claims.quote: Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: The giant was made by George Hull, a tobacconist who was Newell's cousin
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull. ... During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: Hull had lost an argument at a revival meeting about the giants in Genesis
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Chicago sculptors carved the block into a likeness of Hull himself
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant. ... The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles were used to age the surface and simulate pores
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: The hoax cost Hull $2,600
claims.quote: By then, he had spent US$2,600 (equivalent to $63,000 in 2025) for the hoax.

claims.claim: Geologists were not fooled by the giant
claims.quote: John F. Boynton, the first geologist to examine the giant, declared that it could not be a fossilized man

claims.claim: Yale's Othniel Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug"
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue ... and termed it "a most decided humbug"

claims.claim: Marsh argued soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not still carry fresh tool marks
claims.quote: pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did)

claims.claim: Andrew D. White noted there was no reason to dig a well on that spot
claims.quote: He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Hull sold his interest for $23,000
claims.quote: Eventually, Hull sold his part-interest for $23,000 (equivalent to $586,000 in 2025) to a syndicate of five men headed by David Hannum.

claims.claim: P. T. Barnum offered $50,000, was refused, and had a plaster copy made instead
claims.quote: showman P. T. Barnum offered $50,000 for the giant. When the syndicate refused, he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy.

claims.claim: Both giants were declared fakes in court on 2 February 1870
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: The lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant" dates from 1869
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A. L. Edwards, in the Clerk's Office, of the District Court, for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

claims.claim: All the images used are public domain
claims.quote: Licence: Public domain
